openingStatements.speaker: Kim Trowbridge
openingStatements.delivery: written statement read aloud by moderator Dr. Steve Barron
openingStatements.text: First, I sincerely regret that I cannot be with you in person this evening. I am currently in Toronto, attending to private family matters, and unfortunately, I am unable to return. Anmore has been my home for many years, and it has been an extraordinary honour to serve our community as a village councillor for the past 12 years. I am grateful for the opportunity to have worked alongside residents, council colleagues, staff, volunteers, and neighbours who care deeply about making Anmore the wonderful place it is. I hope residents will look beyond the disagreements of the past term and consider the broader record of the past 12 years. There have certainly been difficult moments and decisions I wish we had handled differently, but there have also been many accomplishments, accomplishments of which I am proud. These include the Hub, improvements to our roads, reliable water infrastructure, multi-use pathways, and the financial work that helped achieve 12 consecutive balanced budgets and ultimately a healthy cash surplus. At the same time, public service requires honesty and humility. I recognize that some decisions during the last term could have been handled better. In particular, I regret the use of a procedural bylaw that limited opportunities for community discussion around development. I was pleased that Council ultimately voted unanimously to abolish that bylaw and restore greater opportunity for public discussion. I recognize that should have happened sooner. Looking ahead, I believe the next council should focus on healing divisions and working together on priorities that benefit the greatest number of residents. Three priorities stand out to me: modernizing the public works yard and building a new fire hall; completing the Dr. Hal Weinberg Spirit Park road realignment and expansion; and undertaking a thoughtful, comprehensive update of Anmore's official community plan with meaningful public consultation. Anmore is a special community. We will not always agree, and we should not expect to, but we can disagree respectfully, listen to one another, and work together towards solutions that strengthen our community. After 12 years of service, I really am deeply grateful for the trust residents have placed in me. I have made mistakes, I have learned from them, and I am proud of what we have accomplished together. I would also like to congratulate Councillor Richardson on becoming our Mayor-elect. I strongly support him in this important role and sincerely wish him every success.

openingStatements.speaker: Wade Parrish
openingStatements.text: Good evening and thank you for your attendance. My name is Wade Parrish. I apologize for my public speaking. I only hear my heart beating right now. Those that know me, just being on this stage is a true testament as to how much I care for our village. What makes a village a home? Community. We gather in our limited public spaces: Anmore Elementary, the Hub, Dr. Hal Weinberg Spirit Park, Anmore Grocery, and a big welcome to the Trails Coffee. Anmore is limited by geography. We will probably never have our own ice rink or library, but through volunteering, we create new social networks: Scouts, schools, Sasamat Volunteer Fire Department. More than half of my adult life has been influenced by sharing the Anmore community spirit. I bring with me Anmore's history, a sense of the old ways. I feel what has been lost, and I vow to bring it back. We can create new housing in Anmore that can complement our village. We need to explore affordable housing: smaller starter homes, simple kitchens, unfinished basements, unfenced yards. The young families who purchased these homes could move in and save further upgrades. If the village doesn't lead in this process, affordable housing will never happen. Through proactive thought and villager input, our OCP can guide future development. We should not let developers dictate their vision of our future. My wife Brenda and I have shared countless evenings talking about village problems. These conversations have morphed into, what should we do about it? With her love and support, I have decided to run for Anmore Village Council. Thank you.

openingStatements.speaker: Paul Weverink
openingStatements.text: Thank you. I think a lot of you know me. I've been on council for the last three terms. I've lived in Anmore for 28 years. I've sat on several committees, including some Metro Van committees. I guess I'm the experienced one at the table, which is the reason I'm running. I kind of decided to retire, and a few people approached me and said, look, can we at least have an incumbent or two to choose from? So that's what I'm offering: another four years. I plan to be in Anmore for four more years. I care about this village. I've been here 28 years, raised my family here. I care about everything. I'm proud of what our council has accomplished in the past. I think Councillor Trowbridge spoke of it: the Village Hub, the changes to Spirit Park, and the little things that people don't see: asphalt, drainage, pipes in the ground, an asset management plan that's been put in place to tax fairly, to put money away to replace all the assets. The way the village is run, when something is built or replaced, that gets programmed into our asset management plan. We make sure that it's depreciated accordingly and money is put away. Not every community does that. And I think things like that, people don't realize what council really does. And I know we all get emotional over development, and it was a tough four years. You know, try to sit at the council table going through two huge developments, the biggest we'll ever see. It wasn't easy. And I realize that development is the most important thing to people, and we've got to do that better. We were limited by our procedural bylaw. We were limited by Bill C-44, and we would have done things differently. I was the one that challenged our procedural bylaw, which was based on Bill 44, to just allow more public input. And you know what? The government hasn't come back and taken it away from us. Okay, please vote for me.

openingStatements.speaker: Will Crocker
openingStatements.text: Can you hear me okay? Hello, I am Will Crocker, and this November will mark 27 years I have lived in Anmore. My three children, who are all currently attending university, started school right next door at Franklin Forest Preschool and graduated from Heritage Woods. I volunteered for many school sports and arts programs, officiated Port Moody Old Timers Hockey, happily assessing Anmore's Dave Fardy penalties whenever the opportunity presents itself. I proudly served 13 years with our Sasamat Volunteer Fire Department, including as a member of the Honour Guard and, most recently, holding the position of equipment officer. I have a background in maintaining, operating, and renewing facilities and grounds for local universities and colleges. I'm currently an operations manager for a project that renewed 13 heritage buildings on the Downtown Eastside of Vancouver, enabling housing for over 900 people. I'm advocating that you vote for change in Anmore's council in the upcoming election and vote for me. Some reasons why. If you look back, I took you back in time to when my children were attending Anmore Elementary. On a summer's day, driving to Anmore along Ioco Road, I didn't have to wonder, if there was a forest fire in Anmore, what would this narrow, two-lane street look like if 7,000 people all had to evacuate Belcarra, Sasamat Lake, condo towers in Anmore South, the Village of Anmore, and Buntzen Lake all at the same time? Nancy Maloney, you or I could ask respectful questions at council meetings and sometimes get an answer. The trees your children played around at Spirit Park events were still in the ground. Presently, our village built the Anmore Community Hub with a large room for community gatherings, but here we are in a school gym, unable to use that large community room. I think we deserve better, and I want to be part of that. So vote for me, Will Crocker, and remember, where there's a Will, there's a way.

openingStatements.speaker: Carl Schmidt
openingStatements.text: Thanks, Steve. Good evening. I'm Carl Schmidt. Janine and I moved to Anmore 20 years ago this month into the home we built on Ravenswood. We had no idea we'd be labeled those Ravenswood people because of the half-acre lots, but we love our street. We love welcoming folks on Halloween and Christmas, and we love raising our kids here and volunteering with First Anmore Scouts. About me, I co-founded a tech company called Unbounce. I helped to grow that to around 200 people. I've chaired a board of a 300-student school for about six years. Both of those experiences taught me finance and governance, but more importantly, they taught me how critical good conversation is to making good decisions. Janine and I came here for what Anmore is: quiet, green, and close to nature. And I suspect most of you did too. I truly want Anmore to retain that semi-rural feel. Our next official community plan is our chance to protect that through an open process with real numbers that we can trust. If elected, my experience with budgets, forecasting, and governance can help make that happen. But an open process only works if people feel safe to take part. Many people tell me they don't feel heard at council, and some are genuinely afraid to raise unpopular views. If elected, I'll push to continue to change our procedures so residents have a real voice at council meetings. But even before that, this Saturday at Trails Coffee, I'm recording a live podcast, an open conversation, and everyone's welcome, whatever your point of view, including my fellow candidates. So thank you all for coming out. I'd appreciate your vote on October 17th, and I look forward to meeting more of you tonight. Thank you.

openingStatements.speaker: Rod Rempel
openingStatements.text: Hi, good evening. I'm Rod Rempel, for those that don't know me, and I'm running for Anmore Council. I'm running on three commitments that are based on our official community plan. That's a rule book on how Anmore is going to grow in the future, and it's a time that we need to properly review it, and residents need to be involved in that from the start. My first commitment is open communication. Our council chambers should feel welcoming, not intimidating. When you ask a question, you deserve a real answer and respect. You should hear about things, decisions that are being made during the decision-making, not after the fact. Our community hub is a good example. We paid for it, and many residents are showing concern that we don't get to actually use it, and that's something that we need to change. My second commitment is growth that fits our community. We chose Anmore for its natural beauty and its village culture, and any new development should respect both. It should also pay its own way. Growth should be a financial benefit to our village, not a bill that we end up paying. Before big decisions are made, you should know what it will cost, what it will change, and have your input. My third commitment is wildfire safety. We need to ensure that our wildfire plan is current and acted on. We need a good communication system for when fires occur, and we need to support our fire department so that it's there when we need it to keep us safe. Safety of our community is the first priority of our council, and it's something that I'll definitely work towards. A new council can do things differently, and I would be honoured to be part of that. Thank you.

openingStatements.speaker: Harriette Chang
openingStatements.text: I'm going to stand up because this is a long evening. I've got to get through this evening. So if I stand up, I will. All right, so I'm Harriette Chang, the blonde lady with the Asian last name. I'm married to Warren Chang. Wave, Warren. And our daughters, Taryn and Brayden, [unclear]. They grew up here. We have lived in Anmore for 18 years, and we care deeply about our community. I plan to live here until I am forced into a care home. I am a former school counsellor and teacher of 30 years, and I have dedicated my career to supporting the mental well-being of my students and colleagues in SD43 and at Anmore Elementary School. I used to teach right here in this building. So cool. I'm an experienced facilitator, adult conflict resolution mediator, and collaborative decision maker. And I believe in the possibility of win-win in most outcomes. I do not have a political background. I am really interested in making a positive difference in our community, and for the past 20 years, I've empowered and mentored local youth from Anmore and beyond to present at council meetings to speak about what truly matters to them, including proclaiming annual kindness weeks. I care about. Number one, encouraging and listening to community voice. Creating a welcoming environment for individuals, youth, and community groups to openly share their concerns and to be heard is critical. Number two, supporting sustainable development. By aligning development with a comprehensive, updated OCP, Anmore leadership will be better equipped in making informed decisions on development proposals, protecting our environment, and establishing long-term sustainable goals. Number three, improving emergency preparedness. On August 5th, I experienced firsthand the chaos which ensued when placed on EvacAlert before the fire was contained. Let's have greater communication, organization, and water infrastructure, as well as our evacuation plans. If elected, I promise to listen, represent, and deliver. Please vote for Harriette Chang. Chang for change. Thank you.

openingStatements.speaker: Neil Lyons
openingStatements.text: Good evening, Anmore residents and fellow candidates. My name is Neil Lyons, and I am running for Anmore Council. Forty years ago, a small group of residents, including former Mayor Al Weinberg and Greenpeace President Bob Hunter, crafted a document called the Anmore Concept. It was essentially a declaration of independence in response to the pressure to join Port Moody. At its heart was a desire to create a semi-rural community that would remain outside the Metro Vancouver urban containment boundary, giving people an alternative to the urban sprawl. In 1987, a referendum was held, and approximately 80% of the residents voted in favour, and the village was incorporated. Now fast forward to spring of 2025. Once again, Anmore is under pressure to split off Anmore South and make it urban, thereby changing the look of Anmore forever, but this time with the support of most of council. Once again, you, you the residents, mobilized and stood up for your shared values and single-handedly convinced Icona to withdraw. It was an amazing display of unity and truly a remarkable credit to our community. And now it is election time, an opportunity to right the vote and bring back balance to council. As a director for the Anmore Residents Association, I have worked hard to raise awareness, defend your semi-rural values, and be a voice for those who feel that they are not being heard. Most importantly, I understand the meaning of the word accountability. In this election, we are fortunate to have a lot of good people running for council. I encourage you to carefully review the record of the incumbents and the platforms of the, of the new candidates, and vote for those who best reflect your values. Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.

openingStatements.speaker: Georgia Lyons
openingStatements.text: Hello, everyone. My name is Georgia Lyons, and I have been a resident of Anmore for 20 years. I wanted to talk a little bit about me first, so you can truly get the understanding of who I am as an individual. I am a recent graduate of McGill University with a degree in psychology, and I'm looking forward to starting my master's in school psychology next year. During the last couple of years, I devoted my life to working with kids with autism to help provide support and teach them daily life skills. In addition, I also work for JR Country and 102.7 The Peak as a promoter. I am also the founder of Candy Cane Lane, our local fundraiser that I created during COVID-19. It has brought me so much joy giving back to the community that I want to continue that by running for Anmore Council. I may be young, but I have heart, and I learn quickly. I personally believe that I would be a good asset for Anmore Council because I am a youthful presence that can have a fresh start on this council. My platform consists of community engagement with the village and the residents, open communication and transparency, and emergency response preparedness. For some example, having more events catered to adults. I also think a good idea is having emergency preparedness barbecue, which helps educate residents on what to do in emergency, while also having a local gathering. I also want to allow people as much as possible to voice their opinions, and for the council to be held accountable by being transparent. I want to end on one last note, that even though I do not have as much experience as other candidates, I am a hard worker, fast learner, and really do care for the community. I'm a person that can connect and inspire people, and I believe that is what is missing from our council. If elected, I know for a fact that I would do my utmost best to represent the community. I want to work alongside residents because I truly do care about this village and want to see it thrive, just like all of you do. Thank you.

openingStatements.speaker: Doug Richardson
openingStatements.text: This will be a bit odd, because this was supposed to come first. But anyway, first of all, I want to thank the Anmore— Is this loud enough? I want to thank the Anmore Times for putting this on. They are a volunteer organization. This is their doing. This isn't the village. This isn't the [unclear]. So I'd like a big round of applause. I'd also like to thank Steve for coming out and being the moderator, and for mostly staying [unclear]. And then I think it's really important to acknowledge that there are actually 10 candidates running. The last time we had more than just acclaimed was 2014. So the fact that these people have stood up and decided to represent the village is completely fantastic to me. And, you know, it was hinted at a little bit here. It is not easy to stand up there or sit up there or represent people. And my last thanks was for all of you. This shows to me that we've become a village who cares about—or care about—our village and where it's going forward. And that's so very important. I'm going to touch on that a little bit more. It's important because of the sort of trauma from the last, you know, Icona days and even the hillside days, that Anmore has to come out and make a choice for their council. So it's really important you make the vote. It's really important you tell your neighbours to vote and tell your neighbours' neighbours to vote. So way back when, four years ago, we had, I think, 889 people came out and voted. I would like to set a record. It's so important for council to choose who they want, who they want to be representative. Because when we do the OCP, which many people mentioned, it has to be your OCP. It can't be a group's OCP, somebody else's OCP. It has to be your OCP. We won't always agree. I actually hope that happens. I think you get better decisions with disagreement. So I'm going to put you back to the council, or the future council, to ask your questions. And my last request is: be respectful and kind. Be as tough as you want. Ask whatever you want, but do it in a respectful and kind manner. And I think that will make the village in the future better. Thank you.

questions.topic: Municipal support, distribution, and council submissions for the Anmore Times

questionTurns.speaker: Nancy Maloney
questionTurns.text: Thank you so much, Steve. Am I loud enough? Nancy Maloney. I'm a resident of Old Anmore, [street number omitted] East Road, and we've been there since 1995. And like Harriette, we plan to stay there until we're living in extended care somewhere. I'd like to begin by thanking the volunteers from Anmore Times, the whole team, for organizing this event. And I want to add that an independent community newsletter is an essential pillar of democracy, and we're so lucky to have had the Times for many years. My question for everyone: as a councillor, will you support the Times by contributing to production costs by approving a possible grant application, which was previously refused by a recent councillor? Also, will you remove the recent prohibition of distribution of the Anmore Times at the Hub, and also provide written submissions of your council activities and decisions regarding issues of community concern, as historically has been done for many, many years in the past in our community? So this question is for everyone.

relatedTurns.speaker: Nancy Maloney
relatedTurns.text: Thanks, everybody. Okay, 30 seconds. No more questions. I'm not going to give this opportunity to anybody else. I should have said so at the time. A couple pieces of information. Actually, people probably remember the News and the Now, both of which—the large organizations which owned those papers stopped funding community newspapers. So people who worked for those newspapers founded a new community paper, which is available in many places, most municipal halls. It's called the Freshet. You can pick it up at Shoppers Drug Mart and various places, and at many municipal buildings except for ours. And many municipal buildings are, in fact, providing funding for it. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Paul Weverink
turns.text: I think you know my answer. When the Anmore Times started to get more and more political, we didn't feel it was appropriate to support a politically biased paper. And I think when people vote, they expect neutrality. And the Anmore Times did get a little political. It wasn't just about, hey, there's a lost dog, hey, there's this happening. I would certainly be willing—I would certainly be willing to meet with the Anmore Times team and discuss and come to some sort of arrangement, because I like the fact that a community newspaper is available in the Village Hub, but it has to be fair to all residents and has to represent all residents. That's my answer.

turns.speaker: Will Crocker
turns.text: Nancy, yes, I would support a possible grant for the Anmore Times. As a long-time resident, I do understand and have read some past submissions that were maybe fairly heated or fairly personalized, and [inaudible]. But I think the Anmore Times in the past has done a good job of editing anything out that shouldn't be in there. And yes, I could see having the Anmore Times being distributed locally, if that was at the Anmore Hub or in the vicinity of the Hub. I don't see an issue with that. It's a public position. I think there's also—working for a municipality, you have to be aware that everything you do is open to freedom of information anyways. And that's just the world we're living in. So thank you.

turns.speaker: Carl Schmidt
turns.text: Yeah, no worries. So thank you for the question, Nancy. I did a little bit of research on this and just some fact-finding, and there's some reasonable questions, I think, around the extent to which municipal funds should be used to fund an individual news outlet. And so Coquitlam, I don't believe, does that. I don't believe any of our local municipalities do. That said, I'm absolutely supportive of finding ways that we can support an important independent voice. We just need to do it in a way that's completely above board. And then, as far as distribution, I don't personally have an issue with having the Anmore Times in the Hub. I think that would be very convenient. So that's my position.

turns.speaker: Rod Rempel
turns.text: I agree that supporting our Anmore Times is very important. But, you know, as Paul was saying, if the Anmore Times does, in fact, have political views that are potentially directed towards any individual or whatever, I suspect that's going to be a problem. But knowing what I do about the Anmore Times, and having read the Anmore Times as much as I have, I cannot see any reason why we would not offer funding for it, and I certainly can't see why we wouldn't be distributing it within the Hub. Also, I completely agree with offering up any decisions that I've made, if I were to be elected in council, and to offer up my positions openly.

turns.speaker: Harriette Chang
turns.text: Okay, so I read the Anmore Times frequently. I really enjoy it. I really enjoy how I feel like it unites our community and builds community connectedness. In terms of paying for it, I think we'd have to do a budget review. I don't know enough about that, so I can't say yes. In that role, I really think that putting it in the Hub—I don't see any reason why not. Again, I would love for it to be available, and there's been times that I've gone there looking for it, and it's not there, and I want a copy. So personally, I would love to see that. Maybe there needs to be somebody looking over it, making sure it's not getting too political, but I see no reason why we can't get it out there again. So, yeah, thank you.

turns.speaker: Neil Lyons
turns.text: I would support the Anmore Times. I think that local papers are really important to our democracy. And I don't really understand when Paul says that they're politically slanted. I mean, are not—letters to the editor are often politically slanted? It's up to the reader to sift through that, and if they feel the paper's getting too politically slanted in one direction, they don't have to read it. That's my opinion.

turns.speaker: Georgia Lyons
turns.text: I support both your questions because I'm really for community engagement, and I think that's a huge part. Yeah, overall, I support you.

turns.speaker: Wade Parrish
turns.text: Quite simply, I love the Anmore Times. I've read pretty much every issue, and I've contributed to some issues. It is a reflection of how the village feels, and sometimes people don't like to hear how the village feels. I don't know if that's being biased or not, but I think we have to keep it alive. Funding, yes, and I am a true believer that it's a shame that it's not on the counter of the Hub.

questions.topic: Funding and completing a bear hazard assessment during the first council year

questionTurns.speaker: Tara Self
questionTurns.text: Hello, my name is Tara Self, and I'm a resident of Countryside Village. If the moderator is okay with it, I'd like to put in a plug for advance voting, which is tomorrow, and it is going to be at the Hub. So, starting at 8 a.m. tomorrow, there's advance voting opportunities. But my question is around bears, and Paul, and why you just mentioned bears as part of your answer. So, I understand council this year started contemplating the idea of having a bear hazard assessment done. Many of us are very fond of our furry friends, but we're continuing to see conflict in our community year after year. We're seeing bears being trapped and destroyed because of that conflict. I would say, from my perspective, Anmore is the weakest link in the Tri-Cities in terms of our attractant management, our Bear Smart bylaws. We don't have Bear Smart community status. We haven't done a bear hazard assessment. So I want to know, as council members, are you willing to fund and back up doing a bear hazard assessment within your first year of the council? There may be grant opportunities to fund that. There might not be, and we might need to use budget money. So where do you stand on that issue? Thank you.

turns.speaker: Carl Schmidt
turns.text: Thanks, Steve. That's a great question, and I agree. We love our bears. Nothing but good encounters, honestly, with our bears. But we understand that that's not the case everywhere in the village. And so, fully supportive, obviously budget-willing, to do such a thing. And yeah, because it does start with education. I think in most cases, it's just folks becoming aware of the little things that we can do. So fully supportive, you know, budget-permitting, of course.

turns.speaker: Rod Rempel
turns.text: Yeah, I agree. I'm fully supportive of that, and I have a bear that continues to come through my yard. I've actually taken my gate out now and a fence panel so that he can just go directly through it. But, you know, one of the things that we've talked about in the past is, you know, Belcarra has a garbage retention area, and I don't know if it would be popular with our village, you know, if we were to have an actual area where we bring our wet waste and our garbage to, and we actually staff one person there to do it. I personally would be in favour of it, probably, but I don't know that the rest of the village would be. But I know it would resolve 50 percent of the problem in my neighbourhood. But yeah, I would be 100 percent in agreement with doing any type of research that we can do and program to educate ourselves on what we can do to protect our bears and our community. Oh, and there's a lot of vehicles in our neighbourhood that would be happy about it too.

turns.speaker: Harriette Chang
turns.text: I'm so pleased you brought up this topic. So, as you know, I have an environmental background. I've met with members of the Tri-Cities Bear Aware [unclear] group, as an educator as well, and that was really important for me to take that information and share it with my students. I'm also an avid hiker, and I've had encounters with wildlife, including bears. I was actually—I'm going to stand up and stretch because I'm getting tired. I was actually hiking on a trail by myself, about an hour away from up in the mountain, and I encountered a mama bear with a cub. And she was coming towards me, and she was making these little angry sounds and moving towards me. And I came around a corner, and I just saw her, and I thought, oh. And I thought some colourful things, which I'm not going to say. And I had my hiking poles with me, and I thought, okay, well, I don't have time to grab my bear banger or bear spray, which I had in my pack. It was right there. So I held my, my poles up in the air, and I just kind of started banging them with each other, and every time I banged, I said, go. Anyway, so I share that story because it really resonated with me. We need to really be aware and cognizant. There's bears right there. This is their world. This is their territory. We live on a creek, and it's Schoolhouse Creek North, and it's bear corridors. So we get bears all the time, and I love them. We have names for them. They're all different. They're so cute. Um, so we learned about a lot of things we can do, when I was talking to people, like putting waste in the right places, not putting it out too early. As you know, we know all these stories. We know about what happens to cars. I saw a car a few days ago that had been completely demolished by a bear inside. So I absolutely support this. We need to get it out there more. We need to get more communication, more awareness, more Bear Aware [unclear], so we understand what to do in the case of a bear. So I applaud you for bringing this up. You're speaking my language and my heart, so thank you.

turns.speaker: Neil Lyons
turns.text: I think that's an excellent idea. I really do. I'm not so sure what that would cost. Do you know yourself how cost—would that be cost-prohibitive in any way, or would it be reasonable?

turns.speaker: Tara Self
turns.text: I don't have up-to-date costs, but I work for a neighbouring municipality that's conducted a bear hazard assessment, and it does involve retaining a consultant to look throughout the community at various hazards, whether that's fruit trees or waste management. It's something you can often get grants for, so I think that would be a wise approach, is pursuing grants and perhaps topping off with dollars from the village.

turns.speaker: Neil Lyons
turns.text: May I ask which city or village or town that you knew this was conducted with? This has happened?

turns.speaker: Tara Self
turns.text: [unclear overlap] Yeah, I work for the City of Coquitlam, but many other communities have completed theirs.

turns.speaker: Neil Lyons
turns.text: Well, I only ask that question because maybe we could tag with one of these other towns that have done this assessment and get an idea of what it would cost and get a full understanding of what we would get ourselves into. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Georgia Lyons
turns.text: Personally, I would try so hard because I think it's important. I think it's also important that we have, like, bear awareness workshops and, like, maybe focus on, like, just bringing awareness to everyone, because there's so much that you can know about this. And I feel like, even for me, I need to, like, have more education on it.

turns.speaker: Wade Parrish
turns.text: Well, our bylaw officer could ticket people that are putting out their trash the night before. The bears are getting smarter. I've been in the neighbourhood for about 30 years now. Gone are the days where you could go out the door and yell or hit them with the air horn. They're just staring at you, and it's frightening. And I think it was about five years ago where I phoned the conservation officer, and I said, this bear is different. This bear—I've never had a problem with a bear before—this bear stared me down, and I thought I was in trouble. So they are getting smarter. We have to be proactive in the way we deal with them. I've noticed a big change in garbage collection times. There could be garbage that has been put out at 7 a.m. and picked up at 7 a.m. Right now, our garbage used to be picked up at 7 a.m. Now it's not picked up until 1 p.m. or 3 p.m. So we've got garbage sitting out all day, and it is an open treat. We could have a.m., p.m. rotating days. They wouldn't be able to keep up to our schedule. One side of Anmore, garbage out in the morning; the other side of Anmore, garbage out in the afternoon. I don't know, outside-the-box thinking, but we have to be proactive. As for the assessment, I truly would support that. Anything Bear Aware, anything being to, to save a bear's life, it matters.

turns.speaker: Paul Weverink
turns.text: Good question. So, as the Environment Committee chair, one of the passions of my Environment Committee is Bear Aware. And we did have the Bear Aware coordinator come and meet with us and review what we're doing in the village. And given the size of our village, we actually are doing fairly well. One of the big things is bylaw enforcement. And there are huge challenges around putting garbage out and getting it collected at the right time, as Wade just mentioned. One of the problems is people go to work, and you tell them, okay, your pickup is 11, you put it out between 10 and 11. It just doesn't work. I'm going to talk a little bit about what Rod just said about Belcarra. They do have a compound, and I've heard that it's very successful. So that is worth looking into. But it really, it boils down to people's [unclear] and continuing education, which the village is doing more and more. As far as becoming a Bear Smart community, it's something the Environment Committee supported and council supported.

turns.speaker: Will Crocker
turns.text: Yes, I've also had a few encounters with bears in my years living in Anmore, and they are just amazingly beautiful animals. And so anything to keep bears alive in the community, I'd be in favour of. But obviously there is [unclear] risk. I'm not familiar specifically with the bear hazard assessment, but I am familiar with having assessments done. Anmore, like, we are a small community, and like a lot of small communities across Canada, as you say, a lot of times it's up to the municipality to actually apply for funding, look for those funding sources. And as we do for, you know, a lot of things, looking for grants to repair roads, and I think there was grants for the community Hub, but you actually have to actively apply for those things, and that's, that's part of actively having operations that are involved in that. So, so I definitely do support the bear hazard assessment. Again, it would come down to the cost and if we could afford that. But in the near term, obviously, you know, Anmore is near Belcarra, Coquitlam, Port Moody. We're in the same mountain range, and we have similar problems. So I'd be interested to know if our staff, you know, have shared best practices and are staying on top of those. And then there's always advocacy to the community and continuous education, which, which unfortunately falls to all of us. You know, talk with your neighbours, and as pointed out, you know, if we could have earlier garbage collection, that certainly would help alleviate having the garbage cans out, you know, sitting around for most of the day before they're picked up. So some, some challenges there that we have to keep working on.

questions.topic: Whether councillors will vote with a clear resident majority opposing a major zoning or OCP change

questionTurns.speaker: Michael Tom
questionTurns.text: Hello, Michael Tom, Anmore resident. I think Anmore is a really special community, and I just wanted to open up with that. And I think per capita engagement rate is second to none, as we can see here tonight, relative to our neighbouring communities. So, with that said, the biggest thing for me in this election is voting for a council that will listen to the people that elected them. I'm still in a bit of awe from what happened in Anmore over the last couple of years. Council's decisions seem to keep landing somewhere else than what I thought was clearly the will of the people. So my question is: if a clear majority of the residents oppose a major zoning or OCP change, will you vote with them, or treat that position as something to be consulted and managed? And can you give a personal example that supports your answer?

turns.speaker: Rod Rempel
turns.text: Wow, that is an amazing question. I think we all learned something from the Icona example. I stood in this very room leading a group much the size of what is here right now, trying to get people involved and get them interested in what was actually happening. And we created a survey. We did as much as we possibly could to get people involved. So I can say 100 percent that I want to know what people think and what they want from council. It's—it's, my opinion is one, but there's 2,900 other people here that all have an opinion. And I think, you know, gathering as much information as we can, we get the best resource possible. Anmore is a group of incredibly intelligent people. We're one of the highest per capita income areas in Canada, where half of us are business owners or managers or lawyers or doctors, and—and we need to have our voices heard. So yes, I'm 100 percent behind the fact that I want to know what people want, and that's what I want to go for.

turns.speaker: Harriette Chang
turns.text: Great question. I think that a really big, if not the reason that I'm sitting here today, is because of what happened. So I have always wanted to find answers and ask questions, and I wasn't allowed to. And it goes against every [unclear] of my being. I am a school teacher, a school counsellor. I always encourage my students to ask questions. I always ask questions. I like to model that to them. And they would ask me questions I couldn't answer, and I'd say, 'That's such a great question, and I have no idea, but I'm going to find out the answer for you.' And then the next day, I would try my best to have done that and share that with them. And they would remind me. They'd say, 'Oh, you said you were going.' I did, and here it is. So I think that it's so critical to be allowed to speak and to be heard and to be honoured and respected and valued. So that's why I'm here. I felt like what happened, we were not cared about. I didn't feel that they cared about what I said or what we said. I didn't feel that they respected our values to keep Anmore rural. We were told that there was a silent majority who wished for the development to be passed. I think that silent majority was really, really silent. I don't know who they were. So when we tried to express our concerns and thoughts, we were shut down and we were not allowed to speak. So, for 30-plus years, I've been listening. As a school counsellor, that's how long I did it. I was a school counsellor, and I would listen to students. And I promise you that I would listen, and I would represent, and I would deliver. That's why I'm sitting here. That is the main sole reason, because I'd like to be a part of a council that does the same. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Neil Lyons
turns.text: As far as I'm concerned, if there is a clear majority, I support the majority, even if—even if I feel it's a mistake. That's just the way I feel. It's a no-brainer for me. You made reference to what happened last year, and I think Harriette referenced the fact that they were claiming that there was a silent majority. There was no silent majority. The evidence does not support that there was any kind of silent majority, and that was a false narrative. And it was unfortunate that that came about, and there's nothing more we can do about that. But Icona will be coming back, and we'll get a second chance to get this right this time.

turns.speaker: Georgia Lyons
turns.text: Well, to begin with, I will always listen to the people, point blank. I am studying psychology right now, and I think my goal is always to listen and observe. And I think that's really important when you're on council: listen and observe. You're observing the people that voted for you because they feel like they represent them. So overall, yeah, of course.

turns.speaker: Wade Parrish
turns.text: Oh my goodness, I'm going to quote Judge Judy. We're born with two ears and one mouth, so we should listen. Compromise. I'm the first to admit that sometimes I can be a little bit pig-headed in some of my thoughts, but if I talk to people and I find out that there are more supportive facts on their side, I'm going to change my mind. If I feel that way, if the people that I talk to feel that way, I'm going to stick to my guns. But if the majority of people disagree with me, then I think I do have to change my mind and go with the majority.

turns.speaker: Paul Weverink
turns.text: Yeah, I've spoken about the legislative process, and we all have to follow that, whatever it is, whether it's our bylaws, whether it's government—government. But yes, what council has to realize is there's many different inputs. If you read the OCP, it talks about financial sustainability, it talks about preserving green space, it talks about clustering. There's all these little things, and a lot of things in the OCP are platitudes. So I think in the case of Anmore South, when we got to the point where there was a public hearing, and there was literally—I don't know how many people were signed up to speak—and we know what they were going to say, we knew what we were going to hear, but we needed to hear it. What I'm worried about is a feeling in the community, an atmosphere in the community, of people being afraid to say really what they want. I mean, it's no different in every other community. When you put in a big development, there's going to be loud opposition. There's always going to be groups forming that oppose. How do we hear the people that are for? So it's very, very hard for a council. I don't know if there was ever a majority. I think that more came from the developer, and I'm glad it became a more village-led process later. But of course you're going to listen to it. Ultimately, if you have the feeling of the village and you know that something is not popular, I don't know what any of us would be doing here voting that through. It would die.

turns.speaker: Will Crocker
turns.text: I think, to preface my answer, I want to say that one of the reasons I live in Anmore is because I appreciate the rural landscape that we have. You just don't get this in, you know, a lot of places across Canada don't have what we have with the mountains and being close to nature. And, you know, if I wanted to be in an urban setting, I would move to Moody, Coquitlam, Burnaby. You know, I grew up in Langley. Like, you know, and so I think it's important that, being on council, that we recognize what makes Anmore Anmore, makes it unique. And it is worth, you know, I would say fighting for, or actually, you know, putting forward ideas that help protect that. When I look at supporting something like if the majority had an idea on a change that they wanted, I do look at the process. Is the process set up to get those inputs in a manner that people are comfortable speaking? And I think, yeah, at some point we're going to see—well, I could say the 27 years that I've been here, when I first moved here, I would say that the idea of a third-acre, that was a complete non-starter with the residents that I knew where I lived, you know, on Sunnyside Road. And over time, that changed, right? So that had input from the community, and so you do see a place that, you know, a way that that could change. But I think it comes down to how the process is, that you're getting that input on the OCP, you're getting that input from the community. I may get all the details wrong, but I think one of the—something I observed that I didn't really appreciate was, I was at a meeting about Spirit Park, and there was talk about how did the—how did that plan come about? And, you know, one of the inputs was that there was—I don't know if it was [unclear] Day or if it was the Easter egg hunt—it was a community event. And, and, you know, somebody said, well, they actually—people were able to go up and put a piece of paper in a jar on what you thought should happen in the park. And it didn't say if they were from Anmore, it didn't say if they were with, you know, Port Moody. You could just come and put an idea. And I'm like, really? That—you put that as part of the—part of the solution into choosing that. So I think I'd like to see less of that and, and a better process going forward. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Carl Schmidt
turns.text: Wow, thank you. So this is the sharpest question we've had, and I thank you for it because it cuts to the nature of what our democracy is. And it gives us the opportunity to show you the potential of who you might choose as, as your leaders. So I'm going to throw caution to the wind and step into the grey area because I think truth often exists in that in-between space. So I, I don't like answering in absolutes. We've heard a couple of folks say, yes, I would always vote with the majority. I have a hard time saying, yes, I would always unconditionally vote with the majority. What I would say is that if I ever found it necessary to not represent what I clearly saw as the majority view of the population that I represented, I would be crystal clear about why that was the case. And I think that's something that we haven't necessarily had the opportunity to hear as much from everybody on all sides, is some of the why behind some of the decisions that get made. And so we'll see how this turns out in the election, whether this is something that folks kind of embrace as a more nuanced view of what it means. But that's my—that's my answer, and I thank you for your question.

closingRemarks.speaker: Paul Weverink
closingRemarks.text: I'm going to say kind of what Wade said. I'm actually very heartened to see these candidates beside me. closingRemarks.speaker: Will Crocker
